parse.title: bank
parse.text:
English

Alternative forms

Pronunciation

Etymology 1

Noun

  2. (countable) An institution where one can place and borrow money and take care of financial affairs.
    • 2013 June 1, “End of the peer show”, in The Economist, volume 407, number 8838, page 71:
  3. (countable) A branch office of such an institution.
  4. (countable) An underwriter or controller of a card game.
  5. (countable) A fund from deposits or contributions, to be used in transacting business; a joint stock or capital.
    • 1625, Francis [Bacon], “Of Usury”, in The Essayes […], 3rd edition, London: […] Iohn Haviland for Hanna Barret, →OCLC:
  6. (gambling, countable) The sum of money etc. which the dealer or banker has as a fund from which to draw stakes and pay losses.
  7. (slang, uncountable) Money; profit.
    • 2010, Paul Bouchard, Enlistment, page 113:
  8. (countable) In certain games, such as dominos, a fund of pieces from which the players are allowed to draw.
  9. (countable, chiefly in combination) A safe and guaranteed place of storage for and retrieval of important items or goods.
  10. (countable) A device used to store coins or currency.
  11. (countable, music) A collection of instrument data on a digital synthesizer.
Derived terms
Related terms
Descendants
Translations

Verb

  1. (intransitive) To deal with a bank or financial institution, or for an institution to provide financial services to a client.
    • 1979, Douglas Adams, The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy:
  2. (transitive) To put into a bank (financial institution).
  3. (transitive) To store in a bank (storage).
    • 2013 March, U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, HIPAA Administrative Simplification‎[1]:
  4. (transitive, slang) To conceal in the rectum for use in prison.
  5. (transitive, finance) To provide banking services to.
    • For quotations using this term, see Citations:bank.
Derived terms
Translations

Etymology 2

Noun

  2. (hydrology) An edge of river, lake, or other watercourse.
    • 1599 (first performance), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Iulius Cæsar”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London: […] Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act I, scene i]:
    • 1943 June 8, “Jap Remnants Suffer Heavy Casualties: Alerts In Chungking”, in The Bombay Chronicle‎[2], volume XXXI, number 134, page 1:
    • 2014 September 16, Ian Jack, “Is this the end of Britishness”, in The Guardian‎[3], archived from the original on 13 October 2026:
  4. (nautical, hydrology) An elevation under the sea; a shallow area of shifting sand, gravel, mud, and so forth
  6. (geography) A slope of earth, sand, etc.; an embankment.
  8. (aviation) The incline of an aircraft, especially during a turn.
  10. (rail transport) An incline, a hill.
    • 1940 December, O. S. M. Raw, “The Rhodesia Railways—II”, in Railway Magazine, page 640:
    • 2025 November 12, 'Mystery Shopper', “Is Devon the cream of the crop?”, in RAIL, number 1048, page 48:
  12. A mass of clouds.
  14. (mining) The face of the coal at which miners are working.
  16. (mining) A deposit of ore or coal, worked by excavations above water level.
  18. (mining) The ground at the top of a shaft.
Derived terms
Related terms
Translations

Verb

  1. (intransitive, aviation) To roll or incline laterally in order to turn.
    • 2026 October 2, David M. Halbfinger, Natan Odenheimer, Adam Rasgon, Johnatan Reiss, Aaron Boxerman, “The Mother’s Scream That Sent Passengers to the Rescue”, in The New York Times‎[4], retrieved 5 October 2026:
  3. (transitive) To cause (an aircraft) to bank.
  4. (transitive) To form into a bank or heap, to bank up.
  5. (intransitive, of clouds) To form a bank; to gather in masses.
    • 2011 December 14, Sandra Birdsell, The Chrome Suite, Emblem Editions, →ISBN:
  6. (transitive) To cover the embers of a fire with ashes in order to retain heat.
  7. (transitive) To raise a mound or dike about; to enclose, defend, or fortify with a bank; to embank.
    • 1601, C[aius] Plinius Secundus [i.e., Pliny the Elder], “”, in Philemon Holland, transl., The Historie of the World. Commonly Called, The Naturall Historie of C. Plinius Secundus. […], , London: […] Adam Islip, →OCLC:
  8. (transitive, obsolete) To pass by the banks of.
    • c. 1595, William Shakespeare, King John, act 5, scene 2:
  9. (rail transport, UK) To provide additional power for a train ascending a bank (incline) by attaching another locomotive.
    • 1942 March, “Notes and News: Locomotive Notes”, in Railway Magazine, page 93:
    • 1960 July, “Motive Power Miscellany: Western Region”, in Trains Illustrated, page 443:
    • 1960 September, P. Ransome-Wallis, “Modern motive power of the German Federal Railway: Part One”, in Trains Ilustrated, page 558:
Derived terms
Translations

Etymology 3

Noun

  1. A row or panel of items stored or grouped together.
    • 2011 December 10, Marc Higginson, “Bolton 1 - 2 Aston Villa”, in BBC Sport‎[5], archived from the original on 8 October 2026:
  2. A row of keys on a musical keyboard or the equivalent on a typewriter keyboard.
  3. (computing) A contiguous block of memory that is of fixed, hardware-dependent size, but often larger than a page and partitioning the memory such that two distinct banks do not overlap.
  4. (pinball) A set of multiple adjacent drop targets.
Synonyms
Derived terms
Translations

Verb

  1. (transitive, order and arrangement) To arrange or order in a row.

Etymology 4

Noun

  1. A bench, as for rowers in a galley; also, a tier of oars.
    • 1658, Edmund Waller, he Passion of Dido for Æneas:
  2. A bench or seat for judges in court.
  3. The regular term of a court of law, or the full court sitting to hear arguments upon questions of law, as distinguished from a sitting at nisi prius, or a court held for jury trials. See banc
  4. (archaic, printing) A kind of table used by printers.
  5. (music) A bench, or row of keys belonging to a keyboard, as in an organ.
